Cross-attention driven RGBD fusion in lightweight CNN–Transformer for
real-time stress classification of seedlings during robotic transplanting


Yu Zheng a,1, Seong-Min Kang a,1, Do-Hwan Kim a, Yunde Shen d, Kyeong-Hwan Lee a,b,c ,∗


a Department of Convergence Biosystems Engineering, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea
b AI Agri-Tech Research Center, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea
c BK21 Interdisciplinary Program in IT-Bio Convergence System, Chonnam National University, Gwangju, Republic of Korea
d College of Mechanical and Electrical Engineering, Wenzhou University, Wenzhou, China

A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords:
Plant phenotyping
Seedling vigor
Hybrid CNN–Transformer
Dual-stream fusion
Embedded vision


A B S T R A C T

Timely selection of high-quality seedlings during robotic transplanting is crucial for ensuring optimal crop
growth and productivity. However, accurate real-time seedling grading is technically challenging due to subtle
visual differences among stress levels and the limited computational capacity of edge devices. To address this,
we propose a lightweight RGBD (RGB and depth) multimodal framework for six-level stress classification of bell
pepper seedlings. Our approach integrates a dual-stream CNN–Transformer architecture in which hierarchical
cross-attention modules fuse color-texture cues from the RGB stream with depth-derived geometric cues at both
shallow and deep feature layers. The compact tokenizer rapidly extracts multi-scale fused features, which allow
transformer encoders to capture long-range dependencies, and an attention-pooling head produces class logits.
To validate our algorithm, a dedicated dataset of 1537 paired RGBD images was collected with an oblique-view
sensor during the pick-and-place cycle. Deployed on an edge-device, the network achieves an overall accuracy
of 95.8 % and maintains 5.2 frames per second when integrated into the parallel transplant-control pipeline.
Ablation studies reveal that effective fusion of RGBD channel can improve accuracy by 4.9 % over RGB-only
baseline model, which supports the effectiveness of the modality-aware design. This study integrates RGBD
imaging with an edge-ready hybrid network to provide a practical tool for automated seedling transplanting
and an effective solution for multimodal perception in precision agriculture.

1. Introduction

Greenhouse cultivation has expanded rapidly since the 2000s, cov-
ering at least 1.3 Mha as of 2019, and continues to grow globally,
driven by the demand for stable crop production in controlled envi-
ronments (Tong et al., 2024). In parallel, the adoption of agricultural
robotics has accelerated across various stages of the crop lifecycle, in-
cluding seedling cultivation, transplantation, spraying, and harvesting.
Among these, transplanting robots have received particular attention
for their potential to improve labor efficiency and operational pre-
cision. Transplantation is widely recognized as a critical agronomic
intervention, as the selection and placement of seedlings at this stage
significantly influence subsequent crop growth, resource uptake effi-
ciency, and ultimately final yield. Traditional manual transplantation
relies on the experience of farmers or agricultural workers, but the
process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and often inconsistent, un-
derscoring the practical demand for automated solutions (Otoya and


Gardini, 2021). The emergence of seedling transplanting robots marks
a significant advancement in automation, substantially reducing labor
demands and operational time. Improved transplanting efficiency was
achieved by enhancing the precision of robotic arms, underscoring the
potential of such systems to replicate accurate human actions (Zhao
et al., 2023). However, these robots cannot assess seedling quality,
which can affect crop performance and yield. Developing a system ca-
pable of effectively and accurately evaluating seedling quality remains
a critical challenge with significant practical implications.


A variety of approaches have been explored for assessing seedling
quality, including seedling stress detection and seedling health assess-
ment. Early research on seedling quality classification primarily relied
on hyperspectral and thermal imaging techniques (Lowe et al., 2017).
These techniques effectively extracted plant quality indicators based
on spectral signatures at specific wavelengths. While these modali-
ties provide fine-grained insights into plant biochemistry, they face

several practical limitations. High equipment costs and complex cal-
ibration procedures hinder field scalability, while the resulting high-
dimensional data demand computationally intensive preprocessing and
dimensionality reduction using PCA and PLSR (Sarić et al., 2022).
These factors collectively limit their real-time applicability and ro-
bustness in dynamic agricultural environments. With the development
of machine learning, algorithms such as support vector machine and
k-nearest neighbors have been increasingly applied to process agricul-
tural image data (Attri et al., 2024). Although these methods are more
efficient than early statistical methods for processing data, they have
limitations in multi-class classification tasks and are sensitive to param-
eter settings, which can affect their performance under different condi-
tions. More importantly, the accuracy of traditional methods heavily
relies on carefully designed handcrafted feature descriptors, making
it challenging to select the optimal and robust features from a large
pool of extracted features. Consequently, traditional machine learning
techniques have shown limited adoption in large-scale agricultural
production (Kok et al., 2021).


With the rapid development of deep learning, especially the ad-
vent of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), significant progress
has been made in the detection of seedling quality status. CNNs, by
increasing the depth of the network and applying various convolu-
tional operations, can hierarchically represent data. This capability
makes CNNs particularly well-suited for learning local features and
hierarchical representations in images (Alzubaidi et al., 2021). In di-
verse agricultural applications, several classic CNN-based models have
been extensively employed for disease classification and quality assess-
ment (Samiei et al., 2020). However, CNN architectures struggle to
capture long-range dependencies and the global structure of images.
When processing images with scattered features, it is difficult for CNNs
to effectively identify global context and spatial relationships. Further-
more, CNNs often involve a large number of parameters, particularly
in deeper networks (Alzubaidi et al., 2021).


In recent years, vision transformers have emerged as a promising
alternative that can improve accuracy and learning capabilities. These
models represent a shift from traditional CNN methods and focus on
capturing global context and relationships within image data (Han
et al., 2023). Building on this foundation, many high-performing mod-
els, such as swin transformer (Liu et al., 2021), have been proposed and
have achieved excellent performance in various computer vision tasks.
However, despite their improved accuracy, transformer-based image
recognition models still have the drawbacks of being computationally
extensive and architecturally complex. For small datasets, transformer
architectures perform poorly in the absence of multi-scale feature maps
and robust local feature extraction capabilities (Han et al., 2023).


Accumulated literature evidence indicates that RGB-based appro-
aches have achieved notable advances; nevertheless, their single-modal
nature inherently limits the information captured, restricting mod-
els from representing comprehensive plant traits (D. Li et al., 2020).
Regarding the assessment of seedling quality, analyzing RGB images
of seedlings can help determine their health status. Healthy plants
typically exhibit vibrant green colors, while unhealthy or disease-
affected plants appear yellowish or have spots (Agarwal and Dutta
Gupta, 2018). In addition, depth information can provide valuable
scale cues for analyzing the 3D structure of plants, including leaf size,
shape, and overall plant morphology, which are equally important
for assessing seedling quality (Z. Li et al., 2020). Multimodal data
exhibits both complementarity and consistency, allowing the modalities
to compensate for each other’s limitations and deficiencies. As a re-
sult, the perception and interpretation of multimodal information have
become a prominent research focus. For example, Sun et al. (2022) pro-
posed an attention-based fusion module to effectively integrate RGBD
(RGB+depth) information, mitigating the adverse effects of depth noise,
and significantly improving detection accuracy. In Xu et al. (2021), a
novel approach was introduced in which single-channel depth images
were re-encoded into three-channel images resembling RGB structures.


The subsequent integration of these re-encoded depth images with RGB
data resulted in a significant improvement in weed detection accuracy.


While recent progress in plant phenotyping and vision-based classi-
fication has significantly advanced the field, many existing approaches
remain constrained by their reliance on unimodal data sources. In
particular, they often use RGB imagery or vegetation indices derived
from limited spectral bands. These methods primarily focus on ob-
servable surface characteristics such as color intensity, leaf area, plant
height, or chlorophyll content. Although such features provide valuable
visual cues, they not fully capture subtle physiological stress indicators
or underlying morphological traits that are critical for determining
transplant readiness from an agronomic perspective. Moreover, such
parameters are often insufficient to detect early-stage physiological
stress, structural anomalies, or internal health conditions that are vital
for predicting post-transplant survival. Furthermore, these systems gen-
erally lack the capacity to jointly model surface texture and volumetric
cues, which are essential for evaluating key morphological indicators
such as seedling compactness, leaf curling, stem straightness, and root-
substrate integration. In automated transplanting scenarios, robotic
grippers must rapidly manipulate and assess individual seedlings with
sub-second latency. Consequently, classification models must operate
with real-time responsiveness and detect subtle quality variations that
are often imperceptible in 2D RGB imagery. While hyperspectral imag-
ing and full-resolution 3D reconstruction offer rich phenotypic detail,
their high equipment costs and computational demands render them
impractical for deployment on memory- and power-constrained edge
devices. It is beneficial to have a lightweight, multimodal classification
framework capable of real-time operation on low-power platforms, with
robust cross-modal feature representation and fusion capabilities.


In response to the practical demands of real-time seedling assess-
ment in automated transplanting systems, we present a task-specific
visual classification framework that leverages a CNN–Transformer hy-
brid architecture to fuse RGB and depth modalities. Our approach is
specifically designed to operate under the constraints of an edge-ready
embedded platform, enabling accurate, efficient, and real-time evalua-
tion of seedling stress conditions during robotic handling. The specific
objectives of this study are as follows: (1) To curate a novel stress-level
dataset for bell pepper seedlings, capturing both RGB and depth images
in real-time during the seedling transplantation process; (2) To develop
an optimized CNN–Transformer hybrid architecture that synergistically
combines convolutional feature extraction and attention mechanisms
to enhance training efficiency, improve predictive performance, and
enables computational efficiency suitable for deployment on resource-
constrained edge-device in agricultural environments; and (3) To pro-
pose a lightweight cross-attention (CA) multimodal fusion module that
effectively integrates RGBD data, significantly improving classification
accuracy while meeting stringent computational constraints.

2. Materials and methods

2.1. Experimental setup

2.1.1. Preparation of seedling samples


The design of the dataset is crucial to ensuring the validity and
robustness of model training outcomes. In agricultural research, par-
ticularly in seedling cultivation, one persistent challenge lies in the
limited availability and ambiguous classification of seedlings exhibiting
suboptimal growth. Variations in seedling quality are often driven
by genotypic differences, as well as environmental factors such as
uneven water availability and nutrient uptake inefficiencies (Langen-
feld et al., 2022). Among these, water stress and nutrient stress are
widely recognized as two of the most critical abiotic factors affecting
early-stage plant development, influencing photosynthetic capacity,
root architecture, and overall vigor. To systematically investigate the
effects of these stressors and generate phenotypically diverse samples,
we applied a controlled cultivation protocol that precisely regulated

us to induce a continuous spectrum of seedling stress levels under
reproducible conditions. It also allowed us to construct a well-balanced
dataset capturing a wide range of morphological and physiological
stress states. The resulting dataset enhances both the statistical re-

classification models (Li et al., 2022).


We used the plug tray method for seedling cultivation, specifically
employing 36-hole trays filled with coconut coir—a widely used soilless
substrate known for its good air permeability and water retention.
The seedlings were grown following standard cultivation procedures.
The cultivation environment was maintained in an indoor incubator
with a controlled temperature of 27 ◦C, relative humidity set at 70 %,
and 15 h of simulated daylight provided each day. The water supply
regimen was adjusted according to growth stages: 1 L per application
during the early stage (0–15 days), 1.5 L during the mid-stage (15-30
days), and 2 L during the late stage (30–45 days). The nutrient solution
was prepared using a water-soluble nitrogen–phosphorus–potassium
compound fertilizer (20–20–20). During the early stage (0–15 days),
seedlings were irrigated with a 0.25 g/L solution (i.e., 1/4 strength).
From day 15 onward, the concentration was increased to 1.0 g/L (full
strength).


Table 1 presents the experimental groups along with their respective
water and nutrient supply regimens. The control group, denoted as
W2N2, received a standard regimen of water and nutrients, which
was quantified and administered every 2 days, as the baseline condi-
tion. The experimental treatments were designed to simulate reduced
absorption capacity in seedlings. This was achieved by modulating
the frequency and volume of inputs. As a result, the dataset was
enriched with samples representative of lower quality. For instance,
to cultivate seedlings of diminished quality, the frequency of water
supply was reduced (e.g., once every 6 days for the W6N0 group) in
combination with the suspension of nutrient supply, thereby enhancing
the representational diversity of these samples within the dataset.


This strategic cultivation approach enabled the efficient assembly of
a diverse seedling stress dataset and additionally provided the machine
learning models with a wealth of balanced and informative training
data. Such a dataset augments the models’ generalization capabilities
and predictive accuracy.

2.1.2. Embedded platform and RGBD imaging system


As shown in Fig. 1a, to ensure reliable depth acquisition, the
camera-to-subject distance was fixed at 30 cm, slightly exceeding the
minimum depth sensing range of 25 cm specified by the hardware.
During transplantation, seedlings were grasped by a custom-designed
gripper with a minimized contact area, allowing root visibility without
compromising mechanical stability. Importantly, imaging occurs after
the seedling is lifted from the tray, enabling per-plant data collection
without occlusion from neighboring seedlings. A uniform background
or depth-based segmentation technique is applied to isolate the target
seedling, ensuring clean and consistent inputs for subsequent analysis.


The hardware configuration of the seedling transplant system is
built using the Jetson AGX Xavier (NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara,
CA, USA), an embedded AI platform equipped with an 8-core ARM CPU
and 512-core CUDA GPU, capable of delivering up to 32 TOPS for real-
time inference, as shown in Fig. 1b. This platform controls the robotic
arm and force-feedback gripper for precise transplant operations, while
simultaneously acquiring RGB and depth images using the Azure Kinect
DK RGBD camera (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). The
force-feedback mechanism is incorporated to accommodate variations


in root–substrate block size among seedlings. By regulating gripping
force, it ensures stable lifting without damaging the root substrate,
thereby maintaining consistent imaging conditions for RGBD percep-
tion. The camera captured synchronized high-resolution RGB images
(4,096 × 3072 pixels) and aligned depth maps (640 × 576 pixels) at
5 frames per second, thereby enabling real-time seedling stress assess-
ment. The integrated control interface supports unified management
of all modules, thereby facilitating automated data acquisition and
transplant execution.


Fig. 1c depicts the optimized camera mounting configuration set
at a 35◦ oblique angle, which was determined through kinematic
simulation and empirical tuning. This placement facilitates the simul-
taneous capture of key seedling organs (leaves, stems, root-substrate
blocks), thereby enhancing the completeness of morphological infor-
mation. Fig. 1d depicts a conceptual schematic of the anticipated field-
deployment platform, illustrating the envisioned transplanting work-
flow in a greenhouse setting. In this scenario, a 6-DoF robotic arm
transfers seedlings from a high-density nursery tray to a low-density
tray, demonstrating the potential operational process of the transplant-
ing robot system under real-world cultivation conditions. The overall
control process follows a perception–decision–execution loop. Specif-
ically, after a seedling is grasped and lifted by the robotic gripper,
synchronized RGBD images are acquired and processed on the Jetson
AGX Xavier. The proposed classification network performs real-time
stress-level prediction. Based on the inferred stress category, the con-
troller determines the subsequent transplant action. This closed-loop
design enables seamless integration of visual perception and robotic
control during the transplanting process.

2.1.3. RGBD seedling dataset


A representative subset of the constructed RGBD seedling dataset
is illustrated in Fig. 2, featuring seedlings from six distinct stress
treatment groups after 45 days of cultivation. Each subfigure presents
the RGB image (left) and its corresponding depth image (right), offer-
ing a dual-modality visualization of seedling morphology. The visual
diversity across groups is a direct consequence of the differential water
and nutrient regimens outlined in Table 1, and reflects variations in
physiological responses such as leaf area, extent of chlorosis, stem
thickness, and root plug development.


Specifically, seedlings in the W2N2 group (Fig. 2a), which received
optimal watering and nutrient input, exhibit vibrant green leaves with
broad surfaces and dense canopy structures that are indicative of robust
growth. Conversely, seedlings in the W6N0 group (Fig. 2f), subjected
to severe abiotic stress, display prominent stress symptoms, including
stunted leaf growth, chlorotic discoloration, and reduced foliage den-
sity. Intermediate groups (e.g., W4N4 and W4N0) show more subtle
phenotypic differences, such as slight yellowing or marginal reduction
in leaf area, which are visually less discernible and present signifi-
cant challenges for classification models. This highlights the necessity
for fine-grained feature extraction and robust multimodal fusion to
accurately capture such nuanced morphological indicators.


To improve generalization and enhance model robustness under
diverse visual conditions, data augmentation techniques were applied
to the RGB images for training dataset. These techniques included
horizontal flipping and random adjustment to brightness and contrast
within a range of [0.8, 1.2], simulating varying lighting environments.
The aligned depth map was merely flipped horizontally whenever its
paired RGB image was flipped; no brightness or contrast operations

A total of 2769 image samples were utilized in this study, compris-

group, the dataset was randomly partitioned into training and testing
subsets using an 8:2 split ratio, as shown in Table 2. This division
ensures that the model’s performance can be adequately evaluated on
different datasets while preserving a sufficient amount of independent
data to assess the model’s generalization ability.

2.2. Network architecture

In this section, we systematically presented how to effectively utilize
multimodal data (color and depth) to improve the accuracy of seedling
stress classification, starting from the basic structure. This section
included the RGB-CTA (Convolution–Transformer–Attention) network,
which uses only RGB images; the RGBD-CTA-D (Data Layer Fusion)


network, which combines RGB and depth data directly at the input
layer; and the RGBD-CTA-F (Feature Layer Fusion) network, which
fuses RGB and depth features using CA mechanisms. These approaches
explore different strategies for integrating color and depth information
to enhance the classification accuracy of seedling stress.

2.2.1. Baseline model: RGB-CTA network


We presented a detailed overview of a novel network that combines
CNN and transformer architectures with the aim of improving the
accuracy and efficiency of seedling stress classification. The network ar-
chitecture is summarized in Fig. 3 and consists of two key components:
tokenizer and classifier.


The tokenizer is responsible for rapidly extracting rich feature maps
from the input RGB images using the CRP (Convolutional, ReLU, Pool-
ing) module. Subsequently, to adapt to the transformer module, the
feature maps are flattened into one-dimensional vectors and encoded
with positional embeddings. This step allows the model to focus on
local information at different positions within the feature maps. The
classifier receives the one-dimensional feature vectors with positional
embeddings and passes them through the transformer encoder module
to extract deep-level local and global information about the seedlings.
The output is further refined using the attention pooling module and
then classified using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP).


The design of the entire architecture effectively combines the pow-
erful feature extraction capabilities of CNN with the global context
understanding abilities of transformer. In the following paragraphs,
we will systematically present and discuss the specific design and
functionalities of the Tokenizer and Classifier components.

The design of the tokenizer enables the model to process image

a solid foundation is established for the deeper understanding and
accurate classification of seedling stress.

2.2.3. Classifier module and attention-based pooling


A more detailed overview of the classifier component structure is
shown in Fig. 5. It consists of 7 transformer encoders, layer normaliza-
tion, attention pooling, weighted averaging, and a fully connected (FC)
layer.


The input to the classification module comprises a sequence of fea-
ture vectors output by the tokenizer module, where each vector encodes
a distinct local region from the original RGB input. This sequence is
represented as a tensor of dimensions 196 × 256, corresponding to 196
spatial tokens, each with a feature dimensionality of 256. To retain
spatial structural information, a sinusoidal positional encoding strategy
is applied. This technique assigns a unique position-aware embedding
to each token based on its index in the sequence. By incorporating
these embeddings, the model can capture not only the semantic content
of each region but also their relative spatial arrangement, thereby
enabling more contextually aware classification.


Each transformer encoder in the classifier section follows the archi-
tectural design of the original vision transformer and transformer (Doso-
vitskiy et al., 2020), consisting of a multi-head attention (MHA) layer
and an MLP block. These blocks are further enhanced with layer
normalization, gaussian error linear unit (GELU) activation function,


and dropout layers to increase the model’s non-linear expressiveness
and generalization capability.

2.2.4. RGBD-CTA-D: Data-level fusion strategy


RGBD images combine the color, texture, and shape information
from RGB images with the 3D structural information from depth im-
ages, providing a comprehensive visual representation that enables
the model to understand the scene’s content more comprehensively.
The details captured by RGB images help the model visually iden-
tify different objects, while depth information enhances the model’s
understanding of the spatial position and shape of objects. This data
fusion is particularly beneficial for improving the model’s robustness
under complex environmental conditions, such as changing lighting,
occlusion, and visual noise (Garbouge et al., 2021).


Multimodal data fusion can occur at different levels, including the
data level, feature level, and decision level (Sanchez-Riera et al., 2016).
Data-level fusion treats different types of data as indistinguishable
multi-channel inputs that are directly stacked at the model’s input
layer. Feature-level fusion considers the interrelationship between dif-
ferent modal data in the model’s intermediate layers. Decision-level
fusion independently processes each modal data at the model’s output
stage and then combines the results.


As shown in Fig. 6, we adopted a data layer fusion strategy, where
RGB images and depth images are placed side by side as inputs to
the model (Garbouge et al., 2021). This approach treats the depth
image as the fourth channel of the RGB image, resulting in input


data that includes both color and depth information. The advantage
of this fusion strategy is that it requires minimal adjustments to the
network structure. Only the input channels of the first convolutional
layer need to be adjusted from 3 to 4, without significant changes to
the subsequent network structure.


This basic modification enables the model to leverage depth in-
formation to complement color information, providing a richer data
foundation for seedling stress classification. This strategy allows the
model to learn from both color and depth information and provides
the foundation for subsequent feature-level fusion, further improving
the model’s performance. A series of experiments validate the practical
benefits of this approach in seedling stress classification tasks.

2.2.5. RGBD-CTA-F: Feature-level fusion via cross-attention


While the data layer fusion strategy provides convenience in model
development due to its simplicity and minimal model modifications,
it often fails to fully exploit and utilize the complementarity and
correlations between different modalities (Li and Wu, 2024). To extract
relevant features from different modalities and unique features learned
from individual modalities, the following network structure is designed.


As shown in Fig. 7, we have designed four channels (RGB-CRP,
Depth-CRP, Shallow-Fuse, and Deep-Fuse) in the tokenizer part to
extract features from multimodal data. Two channels (RGB-CRP and
Depth-CRP) independently process RGB and depth data, while the other
two channels (Shallow-Fuse and Deep-Fuse) perform feature fusion
through CA mechanisms. These layer structures provide the model with
multi-scale features ranging from primary edge and color information
to advanced object parts and components.


Due to the significant size variations among seedlings, multi-scale
fusion was introduced when designing the CA channels. The concept
of multi-scale representation has been validated (Li and Wu, 2024).
Low-level feature maps have smaller receptive fields and larger scales,
containing less semantic information and more low-level feature in-
formation, such as edges and colors. High-level feature maps contain
more semantic information and advanced feature information, such
as parts and overall structures of objects. CA channels leverage the
advantages of different receptive fields to fuse RGBD information,
allowing the network to adapt well to various multi-scale targets and
improve classification accuracy.


CA plays a crucial role in effectively integrating information from
different data sources such as RGB images and depth images in both
spatial and channel dimensions, enhancing the quality of feature rep-
resentation and improving the model’s understanding of the data. By
reducing the weight of unimportant features, the network can converge
faster and improve computational efficiency, as shown in Fig. 8.

The CA module integrates features from two separate CNN branches,
one for depth image features and the other for RGB image features.
These features are convolutional feature maps with the same spatial
dimensions to facilitate CA calculations. A query–key–value mechanism
is employed where RGB features serve as the query and depth features
as key and value. The dot product between query and key is calculated,
followed by a softmax function to obtain attention weights. These
weights are then applied to the value to yield a weighted feature
representation. Finally, the output of the CA is summed with the RGB
features to achieve fusion, as follows:

and value, respectively. 𝐹 is the weighted depth feature obtained by

the final fused feature, obtained by adding the attention mechanism’s

This fusion method not only preserves the original RGB features but
also combines depth information weighted by the attention mechanism,
allowing the network to enhance the performance of the classifica-
tion task by learning appearance and scale information from different
modalities. The implementation of this approach significantly improves
the accuracy of the model in classifying seedling images, even in
various environmental conditions, enabling robust identification of
different stages of seedlings.


2.2.6. Training configuration


All training procedures were conducted on an embedded com-
puting platform based on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier, operating
under Ubuntu 20.04 with CUDA 11.4. Model development and training
were implemented in python 3.8 using the pytorch 2.1 deep learning
framework.


The training process was configured with a batch size of 32 and
an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−4, which was scheduled using cosine
annealing with a minimum threshold of 1×10−5. The optimizer adopted
was AdamW, incorporating a weight decay coefficient of 6 × 10−2. To
stabilize convergence, a learning rate warm-up strategy was applied
over the first 10 epochs starting from 1 × 10−6, followed by 10 epochs
of cooling and a total training duration of 200 epochs. Label smoothing
with a smoothing factor of 0.1 was applied to mitigate overfitting and
enhance model generalization. Additionally, automatic mixed precision
was enabled to accelerate training and reduce memory consumption
without compromising numerical stability.


To obtain a reliable estimate of generalization performance under
limited data, we adopted an 80 %/20 % hold–out strategy combined
with stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training portion. Specif-
ically, 20 % of the entire RGBD dataset was sequestered as an unseen
test set and accessed only once for the final evaluation reported. The
remaining 80 % was partitioned into five stratified folds that preserve
the original class distribution. For each cross-validation iteration, four
folds (≈ 64 % of the complete data) were used to train the network,
and the remaining fold (≈ 16 %) served as a validation set for early
stopping and hyper-parameter selection. All data splits were generated
with a fixed random state to ensure reproducibility.

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Performance analysis of fusion strategies

To comprehensively evaluate the impact of multimodal fusion strate-
gies on seedling stress classification, we conducted comparative exper-
iments on three network configurations: RGB-CTA, RGBD-CTA-D, and
RGBD-CTA-F. Quantitative results are reported in Table 3. The FPS was
measured on Jetson AGX Xavier using native PyTorch FP32 inference
with a batch parameter of 1. The timing was averaged over 100
test images and included image preprocessing and inference threads
running in parallel with robotic arm, and gripper control programs.


The performance metrics in Table 3 reveal the relative strengths of
the three fusion strategies in terms of both overall correctness and class-
level discriminability. RGB-CTA sets the baseline with a balanced yet
restricted performance across all four metrics. This outcome reflects the
information bottleneck that is intrinsically present in the single-modal
RGB representation when differentiating subtle stress variations. The
marginal improvements of RGBD-CTA-D over RGB-CTA indicate that
simply appending depth as an extra channel offers limited complemen-
tary signals. It gives some noise reduction or contextual help but lacks
an explicit way to integrate modality-specific semantics. In comparison
with the baseline model, RGBD-CTA-F achieves approximately 5 %
improvements in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. These en-
hancements serve to validate the effectiveness of cross-attention-based
feature-level fusion. By leveraging the complementary cues of RGB
appearance and depth geometry, the network can more dependably dis-
tinguish subtle seedling stress patterns (Sun et al., 2022). The consistent
precision and recall improvement indicates that RGBD-CTA-F enhances
positive identification accuracy. It also improves the comprehensive-
ness of detecting stressed classes, thereby increasing the F1-Score. It is
crucial for fine-grained multiclass stress classification where both false
positives and false negatives carry operational cost.


Regarding computational efficiency and deployment feasibility, Ta-
ble 3 reveals critical trade-offs between model complexity and perfor-
mance. The RGB-CTA and RGBD-CTA-D models exhibit nearly identical
parameter sizes (18.09 M vs. 18.35 M) and inference speeds (7.6 FPS
vs. 7.4 FPS), reflecting their shared backbone architecture with only
minor modifications to accommodate the depth channel. This finding
indicates that merely adding depth as an additional input dimension
incurs only a negligible computational burden. However, it also results
in only minimal improvements in classification accuracy (from 90.9 %
to 91.2 %). This observation underscores the restricted effectiveness of
data-level fusion in harnessing multimodal synergy.


By contrast, the RGBD-CTA-F model, with its dedicated dual-stream
encoder and CA fusion module, increases the parameter count to
23.22 M and reduces the inference speed to 5.2 FPS. While this
represents a 28 % increase in model size and a 31.5 % decrease in speed


relative to the baseline, the performance gain is substantial—boosting
accuracy from 90.9 % to 95.8 %. The dual-stream encoders and
cross-attention fusion introduce additional parameters and computa-
tion to better exploit complementary RGB and depth cues. Importantly,
the model maintains a frame rate above the camera acquisition rate
(5 FPS), ensuring it can process incoming frames in real time without
introducing bottlenecks.


From a computational perspective, giga floating-point operations
(GFLOPs) provide a more direct measure of workload than parameter
count alone. The GFLOPs increase from 8.2 (RGB-CTA) to 8.6 (RGBD-
CTA-D) and further to 10.3 (RGBD-CTA-F). This trend is consistent
with the architectural evolution from a single-stream backbone to a
dual-stream design with cross-attention-based feature fusion. While
RGBD-CTA-D introduces only a minor increase in computation by ex-
panding the input channel, RGBD-CTA-F incorporates parallel RGB and
depth encoders as well as cross-attention operations, which substan-
tially increase matrix multiplications and memory access operations.
The observed decrease in FPS is therefore primarily attributed to the
higher computational complexity and increased memory bandwidth
demand. In particular, cross-attention modules introduce additional
tensor reshaping and attention score computation.


Furthermore, given that the operating frequency of the transplant-
ing robotic arm typically allows several hundred milliseconds for
decision-making per seedling, the marginal latency introduced by
RGBD-CTA-F is well within practical tolerances. These results indi-
cate that the additional computational cost of feature-level fusion is
acceptable, especially in precision agriculture scenarios where mis-
classification of stressed seedlings can incur significant downstream
losses.


Since Table 3 cannot fully represent the predictions for each class,
we further compared the performance of the three models using a con-
fusion matrix, as shown in Fig. 9. According to the rules for plotting the
confusion matrix, the numbers on the diagonal of each matrix (from the
top-left to the bottom-right) represent the correct predictions for each
class. The higher these numbers, the better the model’s performance
for the respective class. We analyze the confusion matrix generated
by the RGB-CTA model on the test dataset, as shown in Fig. 9a,
as the baseline. The RGB-CTA model displays significant off-diagonal
dispersion, particularly in intermediate stress categories (e.g., W4N0 vs.
W4N4 and W6N0), suggesting difficulty in distinguishing subtle visual
differences.


The RGBD-CTA-D fusion approach treats depth and color equally,
without according precedence to modality-specific semantics or dy-
namic relevance. A more detailed analysis of the confusion matrix
reveals that, compared with the RGB-CTA baseline, the variety of
error types has increased, as shown in Fig. 9b. Consequently, this
approach results in information dilution rather than augmentation.
Specifically, several intermediate stress categories (such as W2N0-
W4N0) exhibit more frequent cross-class confusions. This implies that
the incorporated depth channel introduces ambiguities that cannot be
effectively resolved by simple concatenation. This discovery suggests
that naive data-level fusion may inadvertently intensify subtle inter-
class overlaps when the modalities are not adaptively coordinated.
Thus, it underscores the need for more structured fusion mechanisms
to clarify correlated yet distinct stress signatures.


In contrast, Fig. 9c reveals a predominantly diagonal distribution
for RGBD-CTA-F, indicating the model’s capacity to differentiate stress
levels with high confidence. The success of this model can be attributed

higher classification accuracy and reliability. This validates the pro-

seedling transplantation systems.

3.2. Interpretability via Grad-CAM attention maps

To further evaluate the interpretability and visual reasoning ca-
pabilities of the proposed models, we employed gradient-weighted
class activation mapping (Grad-CAM) (Selvaraju et al., 2016) to gen-
erate class-discriminative localization maps. These visualizations help
identify salient regions within the input image that contribute most
significantly to the model’s final prediction, thereby revealing the
internal focus mechanism of different architectures.


Fig. 10 illustrates a series of Grad-CAM visualizations for ran-
dom sample seedlings, highlighting the attention regions across differ-
ent network variants. Warmer colors (e.g., red) indicate regions with
higher contributions to the classification output, whereas cooler colors
(e.g., blue) represent less influential or redundant areas. For each ex-
ample, the predicted stress category and the corresponding confidence
score are explicitly annotated, providing a direct visualization of the
six-level stress classification outcome.


From the results in Fig. 10b, it is evident that the RGB-CTA model
often concentrates on localized features such as root boundaries or


individual leaves. These attention areas are narrow and fragmented.
Although they occasionally align with stress indicators, they often fail
to capture broader contextual or structural cues. This phenomenon
accounts for the model’s confusion at intermediate stress levels. The
heatmaps also reveal that important areas, such as subtle chlorosis
on multiple leaves or combined morphology cues, are not consistently
aggregated. This results in unstable decision regions.


The RGBD-CTA-D variant in Fig. 10c shows more spatially extended
attention compared to RGB-CTA, suggesting that the addition of depth
information does help broaden the receptive focus. However, the at-
tention is still irregular and exhibits scattered high-response patches
that do not form semantically coherent regions. Further, it can be noted
that the dispersed high-response patches did not effectively concentrate
on the cues. This partial integration leads to an inconsistent weighting
of appearance and geometric features. This phenomenon is manifested
as both redundant and insufficient emphasis, which contributes to the
heightened confusion among similar stress categories, as previously
noted and as shown in Fig. 9b.


In contrast, the RGBD-CTA-F model Fig. 10d, which utilizes a CA-
based feature fusion mechanism, demonstrates enhanced spatial aware-
ness. Its attention regions are more uniformly distributed over seman-
tically rich parts of the seedling, including leaf clusters, root collars,
and inter-leaf spaces. Such patterns align closely with human-perceived
stress indicators like leaf chlorosis, growth asymmetry, and shoot vigor.
This suggests that the model is not only learning more relevant features
but also reasoning more effectively by leveraging the complementary
information from RGB and depth modalities.


Overall, the attention visualizations not only support the quantita-
tive performance gains observed in previous sections but also demon-
strate that the RGBD-CTA-F model exhibits satisfactory interpretabil-
ity. This property is important for real-world agricultural deployment,
where model transparency and trustworthiness are essential for user
adoption and decision-making under variable field conditions.

globally distributed yet semantically focused activation pattern across
the entire plant structure, highlighting the most informative regions
while suppressing irrelevant background responses. In contrast, the
ablated models exhibit more scattered or incomplete attention pat-
terns, particularly when either shallow or deep fusion is removed, as
shown in Fig. 12f–h. These observations provide intuitive evidence
that cross-attention fusion improves the network’s ability to capture
discriminative stress features from RGBD inputs.


These results validate that hierarchical CA is essential for maximiz-
ing the complementary strengths of RGB and depth modalities. Shallow
fusion can capture coarse structural cues such as leaf edges and con-
tours, while deep fusion can focus on more detailed information. Their
combined effect fosters robust multimodal feature learning, enhancing
stress classification under real-world variability.

3.7. Ablation study: Impact of fusion direction in CA module

In the design of the CA module, we selected RGB features as
the query (primary feature) and depth features as the key and value
(reference features). This is a common and effective design pattern in
multimodal learning. This pattern allows the model to leverage depth
features to enhance and complement the information provided by RGB
features. In this design, depth features are not simply parallel to RGB
features; instead, they interact and fuse meaningfully with RGB features
through the attention mechanism. To validate the effectiveness of this
design, ablation studies were conducted, and the network structure is
as shown in Fig. 13.


As shown in Table 8, the RGBD configuration achieves satisfactory
performance across all metrics, with an accuracy of 95.8 % and an F1-
score of 95.8 %, whereas the reversed DRGB variant exhibits a notable
performance drop (accuracy: 92.2 %, F1-score: 92.0 %). The perfor-
mance gap highlights a critical insight into modality prioritization in
CA design: employing RGB features as queries yields more effective


attention guidance than the reversed configuration. RGB images in-
herently encapsulate rich semantic cues — such as color gradients,
stress-induced discoloration, and textural variations — that are highly
discriminative for fine-grained stress level classification. In contrast,
depth data, while useful for conveying structural geometry and spatial
morphology, lack the visual semantics necessary for precise query
formulation. When RGB features serve as queries and depth features act
as keys and values (RGBD configuration), the network learns to attend
selectively to spatial regions where depth cues reinforce or contextual-
ize color-based anomalies. Conversely, using depth as the query (DRGB
configuration) introduces semantic misalignment, as low-level geomet-
ric features struggle to effectively interrogate high-level appearance
features in the RGB modality. This misdirection compromises feature
integration and degrades classification accuracy, underscoring the im-
portance of modality-aware role assignment in cross-modal attention
mechanisms.


This finding underscores the importance of query–key asymmetry
in multimodal attention design. Assigning semantically richer features
(e.g., RGB) as the query source enhances the network’s capacity to ex-
tract context-aware correlations from auxiliary modalities (e.g., depth).
This improves robustness and generalization in seedling stress classifi-
cation tasks.

4. Limitations and future work

The CNN–Transformer-based algorithm was proposed in this study
for the classification of seedling stress levels, incorporating a lightweight
CA mechanism to enable efficient fusion of RGBD multimodal data.
Although the proposed method demonstrated competitive performance
in terms of classification accuracy, real-time processing, and embedded
deployment, several limitations remain that warrant further investiga-
tion for broader applicability and technical advancement.


The model’s generalization capacity is limited by the scale and di-
versity of the current training dataset, which primarily includes a single
crop species (bell pepper) under standardized stress conditions with
limited variability in seedling age and environmental context. Such
a narrow distribution raises concerns about domain shift, potentially
leading to performance degradation when applied to other crop types,
natural field environments, or multi-source stress factors. Future work
should therefore focus on constructing a more representative RGBD
dataset encompassing multiple crop species, growth stages, and diverse

environmental settings to improve the robustness and generalizability
of the model in real-world scenarios.


Although the model has been designed with lightweight components
for edge deployment, further optimization is feasible and necessary.
Advanced model compression techniques such as pruning and quan-
tization, along with efficient convolutional architectures (e.g., depth-
wise separable convolutions), could be employed to reduce inference
latency and computational cost. Moreover, leveraging dedicated hard-
ware accelerators such as neural processing units (NPU) would facili-
tate real-time and energy-efficient inference, thereby lowering the prac-
tical deployment threshold and enhancing applicability in agricultural
equipment with limited resources.


In summary, future research should focus on improving data diver-
sity, developing automated and integrated preprocessing workflows,
optimizing network efficiency through model compression, enhanc-
ing cross-scenario generalization, and ensuring adaptability to hard-
ware deployment. These advancements could facilitate practical imple-
mentation and scalability of the proposed visual system in intelligent
agriculture applications.

5. Conclusion

In this study, a lightweight CNN–Transformer framework was devel-
oped to assess seedling stress in real time during robotic transplanting
by integrating color texture and depth geometry through a dual-stream
CA strategy. The network employs a multi-scale tokenizer for rapid
feature extraction, transformer encoders for long-range context, and
attention pooling for compact classification. Model performance was
evaluated on a dedicated RGBD dataset comprising seedlings subjected
to graduated water-nutrient stress treatments and was benchmarked
against several compact vision networks as well as a channel-stacking
baseline. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed RGBD-
CTA-F model achieves an overall classification accuracy of 95.8 %
on a six-level stress dataset, while sustaining a real-time inference
speed of 5.2 FPS. Qualitative and statistical comparisons showed that
the proposed architecture delivered the most reliable stress-level pre-
dictions while keeping computational requirements within the lim-
its of an embedded Jetson platform. Future work will incorporate
model compression for ultra-low-power devices and cross-crop valida-
tion throughout the leafy growth period, thereby enabling continuous
vitality monitoring and more responsive nursery management.

Cross-attention driven RGBD fusion in lightweight CNN–Transformer for
real-time stress classification of seedlings during robotic transplanting

Yu Zheng a,1, Seong-Min Kang a,1, Do-Hwan Kim a, Yunde Shen d, Kyeong-Hwan Lee a,b,c ,∗

A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords:
Plant phenotyping
Seedling vigor
Hybrid CNN–Transformer
Dual-stream fusion
Embedded vision

# A B S T R A C T

Timely selection of high-quality seedlings during robotic transplanting is crucial for ensuring optimal crop
growth and productivity. However, accurate real-time seedling grading is technically challenging due to subtle
visual differences among stress levels and the limited computational capacity of edge devices. To address this,
we propose a lightweight RGBD (RGB and depth) multimodal framework for six-level stress classification of bell
pepper seedlings. Our approach integrates a dual-stream CNN–Transformer architecture in which hierarchical
cross-attention modules fuse color-texture cues from the RGB stream with depth-derived geometric cues at both
shallow and deep feature layers. The compact tokenizer rapidly extracts multi-scale fused features, which allow
transformer encoders to capture long-range dependencies, and an attention-pooling head produces class logits.
To validate our algorithm, a dedicated dataset of 1537 paired RGBD images was collected with an oblique-view
sensor during the pick-and-place cycle. Deployed on an edge-device, the network achieves an overall accuracy
of 95.8 % and maintains 5.2 frames per second when integrated into the parallel transplant-control pipeline.
Ablation studies reveal that effective fusion of RGBD channel can improve accuracy by 4.9 % over RGB-only
baseline model, which supports the effectiveness of the modality-aware design. This study integrates RGBD
imaging with an edge-ready hybrid network to provide a practical tool for automated seedling transplanting
and an effective solution for multimodal perception in precision agriculture.

# 1. Introduction

Greenhouse cultivation has expanded rapidly since the 2000s, cov-
ering at least 1.3 Mha as of 2019, and continues to grow globally,
driven by the demand for stable crop production in controlled envi-
ronments (Tong et al., 2024). In parallel, the adoption of agricultural
robotics has accelerated across various stages of the crop lifecycle, in-
cluding seedling cultivation, transplantation, spraying, and harvesting.
Among these, transplanting robots have received particular attention
for their potential to improve labor efficiency and operational pre-
cision. Transplantation is widely recognized as a critical agronomic
intervention, as the selection and placement of seedlings at this stage
significantly influence subsequent crop growth, resource uptake effi-
ciency, and ultimately final yield. Traditional manual transplantation
relies on the experience of farmers or agricultural workers, but the
process is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and often inconsistent, un-
derscoring the practical demand for automated solutions (Otoya and

Gardini, 2021). The emergence of seedling transplanting robots marks
a significant advancement in automation, substantially reducing labor
demands and operational time. Improved transplanting efficiency was
achieved by enhancing the precision of robotic arms, underscoring the
potential of such systems to replicate accurate human actions (Zhao
et al., 2023). However, these robots cannot assess seedling quality,
which can affect crop performance and yield. Developing a system ca-
pable of effectively and accurately evaluating seedling quality remains
a critical challenge with significant practical implications.

A variety of approaches have been explored for assessing seedling
quality, including seedling stress detection and seedling health assess-
ment. Early research on seedling quality classification primarily relied
on hyperspectral and thermal imaging techniques (Lowe et al., 2017).
These techniques effectively extracted plant quality indicators based
on spectral signatures at specific wavelengths. While these modali-
ties provide fine-grained insights into plant biochemistry, they face

several practical limitations. High equipment costs and complex cal-
ibration procedures hinder field scalability, while the resulting high-
dimensional data demand computationally intensive preprocessing and
dimensionality reduction using PCA and PLSR (Sarić et al., 2022).
These factors collectively limit their real-time applicability and ro-
bustness in dynamic agricultural environments. With the development
of machine learning, algorithms such as support vector machine and
k-nearest neighbors have been increasingly applied to process agricul-
tural image data (Attri et al., 2024). Although these methods are more
efficient than early statistical methods for processing data, they have
limitations in multi-class classification tasks and are sensitive to param-
eter settings, which can affect their performance under different condi-
tions. More importantly, the accuracy of traditional methods heavily
relies on carefully designed handcrafted feature descriptors, making
it challenging to select the optimal and robust features from a large
pool of extracted features. Consequently, traditional machine learning
techniques have shown limited adoption in large-scale agricultural
production (Kok et al., 2021).

With the rapid development of deep learning, especially the ad-
vent of convolutional neural networks (CNNs), significant progress
has been made in the detection of seedling quality status. CNNs, by
increasing the depth of the network and applying various convolu-
tional operations, can hierarchically represent data. This capability
makes CNNs particularly well-suited for learning local features and
hierarchical representations in images (Alzubaidi et al., 2021). In di-
verse agricultural applications, several classic CNN-based models have
been extensively employed for disease classification and quality assess-
ment (Samiei et al., 2020). However, CNN architectures struggle to
capture long-range dependencies and the global structure of images.
When processing images with scattered features, it is difficult for CNNs
to effectively identify global context and spatial relationships. Further-
more, CNNs often involve a large number of parameters, particularly
in deeper networks (Alzubaidi et al., 2021).

In recent years, vision transformers have emerged as a promising
alternative that can improve accuracy and learning capabilities. These
models represent a shift from traditional CNN methods and focus on
capturing global context and relationships within image data (Han
et al., 2023). Building on this foundation, many high-performing mod-
els, such as swin transformer (Liu et al., 2021), have been proposed and
have achieved excellent performance in various computer vision tasks.
However, despite their improved accuracy, transformer-based image
recognition models still have the drawbacks of being computationally
extensive and architecturally complex. For small datasets, transformer
architectures perform poorly in the absence of multi-scale feature maps
and robust local feature extraction capabilities (Han et al., 2023).

Accumulated literature evidence indicates that RGB-based appro-
aches have achieved notable advances; nevertheless, their single-modal
nature inherently limits the information captured, restricting mod-
els from representing comprehensive plant traits (D. Li et al., 2020).
Regarding the assessment of seedling quality, analyzing RGB images
of seedlings can help determine their health status. Healthy plants
typically exhibit vibrant green colors, while unhealthy or disease-
affected plants appear yellowish or have spots (Agarwal and Dutta
Gupta, 2018). In addition, depth information can provide valuable
scale cues for analyzing the 3D structure of plants, including leaf size,
shape, and overall plant morphology, which are equally important
for assessing seedling quality (Z. Li et al., 2020). Multimodal data
exhibits both complementarity and consistency, allowing the modalities
to compensate for each other’s limitations and deficiencies. As a re-
sult, the perception and interpretation of multimodal information have
become a prominent research focus. For example, Sun et al. (2022) pro-
posed an attention-based fusion module to effectively integrate RGBD
(RGB+depth) information, mitigating the adverse effects of depth noise,
and significantly improving detection accuracy. In Xu et al. (2021), a
novel approach was introduced in which single-channel depth images
were re-encoded into three-channel images resembling RGB structures.

# The subsequent integration of these re-encoded depth images with RGB
data resulted in a significant improvement in weed detection accuracy.

While recent progress in plant phenotyping and vision-based classi-
fication has significantly advanced the field, many existing approaches
remain constrained by their reliance on unimodal data sources. In
particular, they often use RGB imagery or vegetation indices derived
from limited spectral bands. These methods primarily focus on ob-
servable surface characteristics such as color intensity, leaf area, plant
height, or chlorophyll content. Although such features provide valuable
visual cues, they not fully capture subtle physiological stress indicators
or underlying morphological traits that are critical for determining
transplant readiness from an agronomic perspective. Moreover, such
parameters are often insufficient to detect early-stage physiological
stress, structural anomalies, or internal health conditions that are vital
for predicting post-transplant survival. Furthermore, these systems gen-
erally lack the capacity to jointly model surface texture and volumetric
cues, which are essential for evaluating key morphological indicators
such as seedling compactness, leaf curling, stem straightness, and root-
substrate integration. In automated transplanting scenarios, robotic
grippers must rapidly manipulate and assess individual seedlings with
sub-second latency. Consequently, classification models must operate
with real-time responsiveness and detect subtle quality variations that
are often imperceptible in 2D RGB imagery. While hyperspectral imag-
ing and full-resolution 3D reconstruction offer rich phenotypic detail,
their high equipment costs and computational demands render them
impractical for deployment on memory- and power-constrained edge
devices. It is beneficial to have a lightweight, multimodal classification
framework capable of real-time operation on low-power platforms, with
robust cross-modal feature representation and fusion capabilities.

In response to the practical demands of real-time seedling assess-
ment in automated transplanting systems, we present a task-specific
visual classification framework that leverages a CNN–Transformer hy-
brid architecture to fuse RGB and depth modalities. Our approach is
specifically designed to operate under the constraints of an edge-ready
embedded platform, enabling accurate, efficient, and real-time evalua-
tion of seedling stress conditions during robotic handling. The specific
objectives of this study are as follows: (1) To curate a novel stress-level
dataset for bell pepper seedlings, capturing both RGB and depth images
in real-time during the seedling transplantation process; (2) To develop
an optimized CNN–Transformer hybrid architecture that synergistically
combines convolutional feature extraction and attention mechanisms
to enhance training efficiency, improve predictive performance, and
enables computational efficiency suitable for deployment on resource-
constrained edge-device in agricultural environments; and (3) To pro-
pose a lightweight cross-attention (CA) multimodal fusion module that
effectively integrates RGBD data, significantly improving classification
accuracy while meeting stringent computational constraints.

2. Materials and methods

# 2.1. Experimental setup

2.1.1. Preparation of seedling samples

The design of the dataset is crucial to ensuring the validity and
robustness of model training outcomes. In agricultural research, par-
ticularly in seedling cultivation, one persistent challenge lies in the
limited availability and ambiguous classification of seedlings exhibiting
suboptimal growth. Variations in seedling quality are often driven
by genotypic differences, as well as environmental factors such as
uneven water availability and nutrient uptake inefficiencies (Langen-
feld et al., 2022). Among these, water stress and nutrient stress are
widely recognized as two of the most critical abiotic factors affecting
early-stage plant development, influencing photosynthetic capacity,
root architecture, and overall vigor. To systematically investigate the
effects of these stressors and generate phenotypically diverse samples,
we applied a controlled cultivation protocol that precisely regulated

watering frequency and nutrient supply levels. This strategy enabled
us to induce a continuous spectrum of seedling stress levels under
reproducible conditions. It also allowed us to construct a well-balanced
dataset capturing a wide range of morphological and physiological
stress states. The resulting dataset enhances both the statistical re-
liability and diversity of representational needed for training robust
classification models (Li et al., 2022).

We used the plug tray method for seedling cultivation, specifically
employing 36-hole trays filled with coconut coir—a widely used soilless
substrate known for its good air permeability and water retention.
The seedlings were grown following standard cultivation procedures.
The cultivation environment was maintained in an indoor incubator
with a controlled temperature of 27 ◦C, relative humidity set at 70 %,
and 15 h of simulated daylight provided each day. The water supply
regimen was adjusted according to growth stages: 1 L per application
during the early stage (0–15 days), 1.5 L during the mid-stage (15-30
days), and 2 L during the late stage (30–45 days). The nutrient solution
was prepared using a water-soluble nitrogen–phosphorus–potassium
compound fertilizer (20–20–20). During the early stage (0–15 days),
seedlings were irrigated with a 0.25 g/L solution (i.e., 1/4 strength).
From day 15 onward, the concentration was increased to 1.0 g/L (full
strength).

Table 1 presents the experimental groups along with their respective
water and nutrient supply regimens. The control group, denoted as
W2N2, received a standard regimen of water and nutrients, which
was quantified and administered every 2 days, as the baseline condi-
tion. The experimental treatments were designed to simulate reduced
absorption capacity in seedlings. This was achieved by modulating
the frequency and volume of inputs. As a result, the dataset was
enriched with samples representative of lower quality. For instance,
to cultivate seedlings of diminished quality, the frequency of water
supply was reduced (e.g., once every 6 days for the W6N0 group) in
combination with the suspension of nutrient supply, thereby enhancing
the representational diversity of these samples within the dataset.

This strategic cultivation approach enabled the efficient assembly of
a diverse seedling stress dataset and additionally provided the machine
learning models with a wealth of balanced and informative training
data. Such a dataset augments the models’ generalization capabilities
and predictive accuracy.

# 2.1.2. Embedded platform and RGBD imaging system

As shown in Fig. 1a, to ensure reliable depth acquisition, the
camera-to-subject distance was fixed at 30 cm, slightly exceeding the
minimum depth sensing range of 25 cm specified by the hardware.
During transplantation, seedlings were grasped by a custom-designed
gripper with a minimized contact area, allowing root visibility without
compromising mechanical stability. Importantly, imaging occurs after
the seedling is lifted from the tray, enabling per-plant data collection
without occlusion from neighboring seedlings. A uniform background
or depth-based segmentation technique is applied to isolate the target
seedling, ensuring clean and consistent inputs for subsequent analysis.

The hardware configuration of the seedling transplant system is
built using the Jetson AGX Xavier (NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara,
CA, USA), an embedded AI platform equipped with an 8-core ARM CPU
and 512-core CUDA GPU, capable of delivering up to 32 TOPS for real-
time inference, as shown in Fig. 1b. This platform controls the robotic
arm and force-feedback gripper for precise transplant operations, while
simultaneously acquiring RGB and depth images using the Azure Kinect
DK RGBD camera (Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, WA, USA). The
force-feedback mechanism is incorporated to accommodate variations

in root–substrate block size among seedlings. By regulating gripping
force, it ensures stable lifting without damaging the root substrate,
thereby maintaining consistent imaging conditions for RGBD percep-
tion. The camera captured synchronized high-resolution RGB images
(4,096 × 3072 pixels) and aligned depth maps (640 × 576 pixels) at
5 frames per second, thereby enabling real-time seedling stress assess-
ment. The integrated control interface supports unified management
of all modules, thereby facilitating automated data acquisition and
transplant execution.

Fig. 1c depicts the optimized camera mounting configuration set
at a 35◦ oblique angle, which was determined through kinematic
simulation and empirical tuning. This placement facilitates the simul-
taneous capture of key seedling organs (leaves, stems, root-substrate
blocks), thereby enhancing the completeness of morphological infor-
mation. Fig. 1d depicts a conceptual schematic of the anticipated field-
deployment platform, illustrating the envisioned transplanting work-
flow in a greenhouse setting. In this scenario, a 6-DoF robotic arm
transfers seedlings from a high-density nursery tray to a low-density
tray, demonstrating the potential operational process of the transplant-
ing robot system under real-world cultivation conditions. The overall
control process follows a perception–decision–execution loop. Specif-
ically, after a seedling is grasped and lifted by the robotic gripper,
synchronized RGBD images are acquired and processed on the Jetson
AGX Xavier. The proposed classification network performs real-time
stress-level prediction. Based on the inferred stress category, the con-
troller determines the subsequent transplant action. This closed-loop
design enables seamless integration of visual perception and robotic
control during the transplanting process.

# 2.2. Network architecture

In this section, we systematically presented how to effectively utilize
multimodal data (color and depth) to improve the accuracy of seedling
stress classification, starting from the basic structure. This section
included the RGB-CTA (Convolution–Transformer–Attention) network,
which uses only RGB images; the RGBD-CTA-D (Data Layer Fusion)

network, which combines RGB and depth data directly at the input
layer; and the RGBD-CTA-F (Feature Layer Fusion) network, which
fuses RGB and depth features using CA mechanisms. These approaches
explore different strategies for integrating color and depth information
to enhance the classification accuracy of seedling stress.

# 2.2.1. Baseline model: RGB-CTA network

We presented a detailed overview of a novel network that combines
CNN and transformer architectures with the aim of improving the
accuracy and efficiency of seedling stress classification. The network ar-
chitecture is summarized in Fig. 3 and consists of two key components:
tokenizer and classifier.

The tokenizer is responsible for rapidly extracting rich feature maps
from the input RGB images using the CRP (Convolutional, ReLU, Pool-
ing) module. Subsequently, to adapt to the transformer module, the
feature maps are flattened into one-dimensional vectors and encoded
with positional embeddings. This step allows the model to focus on
local information at different positions within the feature maps. The
classifier receives the one-dimensional feature vectors with positional
embeddings and passes them through the transformer encoder module
to extract deep-level local and global information about the seedlings.
The output is further refined using the attention pooling module and
then classified using a multi-layer perceptron (MLP).

The design of the entire architecture effectively combines the pow-
erful feature extraction capabilities of CNN with the global context
understanding abilities of transformer. In the following paragraphs,
we will systematically present and discuss the specific design and
functionalities of the Tokenizer and Classifier components.

The input to the classification module comprises a sequence of fea-

a distinct local region from the original RGB input. This sequence is

is applied. This technique assigns a unique position-aware embedding

enabling more contextually aware classification.

# 2.2.4. RGBD-CTA-D: Data-level fusion strategy

RGBD images combine the color, texture, and shape information
from RGB images with the 3D structural information from depth im-
ages, providing a comprehensive visual representation that enables
the model to understand the scene’s content more comprehensively.
The details captured by RGB images help the model visually iden-
tify different objects, while depth information enhances the model’s
understanding of the spatial position and shape of objects. This data
fusion is particularly beneficial for improving the model’s robustness
under complex environmental conditions, such as changing lighting,
occlusion, and visual noise (Garbouge et al., 2021).

Multimodal data fusion can occur at different levels, including the
data level, feature level, and decision level (Sanchez-Riera et al., 2016).
Data-level fusion treats different types of data as indistinguishable
multi-channel inputs that are directly stacked at the model’s input
layer. Feature-level fusion considers the interrelationship between dif-
ferent modal data in the model’s intermediate layers. Decision-level
fusion independently processes each modal data at the model’s output
stage and then combines the results.

As shown in Fig. 6, we adopted a data layer fusion strategy, where
RGB images and depth images are placed side by side as inputs to
the model (Garbouge et al., 2021). This approach treats the depth
image as the fourth channel of the RGB image, resulting in input

data that includes both color and depth information. The advantage
of this fusion strategy is that it requires minimal adjustments to the
network structure. Only the input channels of the first convolutional
layer need to be adjusted from 3 to 4, without significant changes to
the subsequent network structure.

This basic modification enables the model to leverage depth in-
formation to complement color information, providing a richer data
foundation for seedling stress classification. This strategy allows the
model to learn from both color and depth information and provides
the foundation for subsequent feature-level fusion, further improving
the model’s performance. A series of experiments validate the practical
benefits of this approach in seedling stress classification tasks.

# 2.2.5. RGBD-CTA-F: Feature-level fusion via cross-attention

While the data layer fusion strategy provides convenience in model
development due to its simplicity and minimal model modifications,
it often fails to fully exploit and utilize the complementarity and
correlations between different modalities (Li and Wu, 2024). To extract
relevant features from different modalities and unique features learned
from individual modalities, the following network structure is designed.

As shown in Fig. 7, we have designed four channels (RGB-CRP,
Depth-CRP, Shallow-Fuse, and Deep-Fuse) in the tokenizer part to
extract features from multimodal data. Two channels (RGB-CRP and
Depth-CRP) independently process RGB and depth data, while the other
two channels (Shallow-Fuse and Deep-Fuse) perform feature fusion
through CA mechanisms. These layer structures provide the model with
multi-scale features ranging from primary edge and color information
to advanced object parts and components.

Due to the significant size variations among seedlings, multi-scale
fusion was introduced when designing the CA channels. The concept
of multi-scale representation has been validated (Li and Wu, 2024).
Low-level feature maps have smaller receptive fields and larger scales,
containing less semantic information and more low-level feature in-
formation, such as edges and colors. High-level feature maps contain
more semantic information and advanced feature information, such
as parts and overall structures of objects. CA channels leverage the
advantages of different receptive fields to fuse RGBD information,
allowing the network to adapt well to various multi-scale targets and
improve classification accuracy.

CA plays a crucial role in effectively integrating information from
different data sources such as RGB images and depth images in both
spatial and channel dimensions, enhancing the quality of feature rep-
resentation and improving the model’s understanding of the data. By
reducing the weight of unimportant features, the network can converge
faster and improve computational efficiency, as shown in Fig. 8.

# 2.2.6. Training configuration

All training procedures were conducted on an embedded com-
puting platform based on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier, operating
under Ubuntu 20.04 with CUDA 11.4. Model development and training
were implemented in python 3.8 using the pytorch 2.1 deep learning
framework.

The training process was configured with a batch size of 32 and
an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−4, which was scheduled using cosine
annealing with a minimum threshold of 1×10−5. The optimizer adopted
was AdamW, incorporating a weight decay coefficient of 6 × 10−2. To
stabilize convergence, a learning rate warm-up strategy was applied
over the first 10 epochs starting from 1 × 10−6, followed by 10 epochs
of cooling and a total training duration of 200 epochs. Label smoothing
with a smoothing factor of 0.1 was applied to mitigate overfitting and
enhance model generalization. Additionally, automatic mixed precision
was enabled to accelerate training and reduce memory consumption
without compromising numerical stability.

To obtain a reliable estimate of generalization performance under
limited data, we adopted an 80 %/20 % hold–out strategy combined
with stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training portion. Specif-
ically, 20 % of the entire RGBD dataset was sequestered as an unseen
test set and accessed only once for the final evaluation reported. The
remaining 80 % was partitioned into five stratified folds that preserve
the original class distribution. For each cross-validation iteration, four
folds (≈ 64 % of the complete data) were used to train the network,
and the remaining fold (≈ 16 %) served as a validation set for early
stopping and hyper-parameter selection. All data splits were generated
with a fixed random state to ensure reproducibility.
