content.text: 2.2.4. RGBD-CTA-D: Data-level fusion strategy

content.html:
RGBD images combine the color, texture, and shape information
from RGB images with the 3D structural information from depth im-
ages, providing a comprehensive visual representation that enables
the model to understand the scene’s content more comprehensively.
The details captured by RGB images help the model visually iden-
tify different objects, while depth information enhances the model’s
understanding of the spatial position and shape of objects. This data
fusion is particularly beneficial for improving the model’s robustness
under complex environmental conditions, such as changing lighting,
occlusion, and visual noise (Garbouge et al., 2021).

Multimodal data fusion can occur at different levels, including the
data level, feature level, and decision level (Sanchez-Riera et al., 2016).
Data-level fusion treats different types of data as indistinguishable
multi-channel inputs that are directly stacked at the model’s input
layer. Feature-level fusion considers the interrelationship between dif-
ferent modal data in the model’s intermediate layers. Decision-level
fusion independently processes each modal data at the model’s output
stage and then combines the results.

content.html:
As shown in Fig. 7, we have designed four channels (RGB-CRP,
Depth-CRP, Shallow-Fuse, and Deep-Fuse) in the tokenizer part to
extract features from multimodal data. Two channels (RGB-CRP and
Depth-CRP) independently process RGB and depth data, while the other
two channels (Shallow-Fuse and Deep-Fuse) perform feature fusion
through CA mechanisms. These layer structures provide the model with
multi-scale features ranging from primary edge and color information
to advanced object parts and components.

content.html:
Due to the significant size variations among seedlings, multi-scale
fusion was introduced when designing the CA channels. The concept
of multi-scale representation has been validated (Li and Wu, 2024).
Low-level feature maps have smaller receptive fields and larger scales,
containing less semantic information and more low-level feature in-
formation, such as edges and colors. High-level feature maps contain
more semantic information and advanced feature information, such
as parts and overall structures of objects. CA channels leverage the
advantages of different receptive fields to fuse RGBD information,
allowing the network to adapt well to various multi-scale targets and
improve classification accuracy.

content.html:
The CA module integrates features from two separate CNN branches,
one for depth image features and the other for RGB image features.
These features are convolutional feature maps with the same spatial
dimensions to facilitate CA calculations. A query–key–value mechanism
is employed where RGB features serve as the query and depth features
as key and value. The dot product between query and key is calculated,
followed by a softmax function to obtain attention weights. These
weights are then applied to the value to yield a weighted feature
representation. Finally, the output of the CA is summed with the RGB
features to achieve fusion, as follows:

were implemented in python 3.8 using the pytorch 2.1 deep learning

content.text:
All training procedures were conducted on an embedded com-
puting platform based on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Xavier, operating
under Ubuntu 20.04 with CUDA 11.4. Model development and training
were implemented in python 3.8 using the pytorch 2.1 deep learning
framework.

content.html:
The training process was configured with a batch size of 32 and
an initial learning rate of 5 × 10−4, which was scheduled using cosine
annealing with a minimum threshold of 1×10−5. The optimizer adopted
was AdamW, incorporating a weight decay coefficient of 6 × 10−2. To
stabilize convergence, a learning rate warm-up strategy was applied
over the first 10 epochs starting from 1 × 10−6, followed by 10 epochs
of cooling and a total training duration of 200 epochs. Label smoothing
with a smoothing factor of 0.1 was applied to mitigate overfitting and
enhance model generalization. Additionally, automatic mixed precision
was enabled to accelerate training and reduce memory consumption
without compromising numerical stability.

To obtain a reliable estimate of generalization performance under
limited data, we adopted an 80 %/20 % hold–out strategy combined
with stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training portion. Specif-
ically, 20 % of the entire RGBD dataset was sequestered as an unseen
test set and accessed only once for the final evaluation reported. The
remaining 80 % was partitioned into five stratified folds that preserve
the original class distribution. For each cross-validation iteration, four
folds (≈ 64 % of the complete data) were used to train the network,
and the remaining fold (≈ 16 %) served as a validation set for early
stopping and hyper-parameter selection. All data splits were generated
with a fixed random state to ensure reproducibility.

content.html: 3.1. Performance analysis of fusion strategies
content.markdown: # 3.1. Performance analysis of fusion strategies
content.text: 3.1. Performance analysis of fusion strategies

content.html:
To comprehensively evaluate the impact of multimodal fusion strate-
gies on seedling stress classification, we conducted comparative exper-
iments on three network configurations: RGB-CTA, RGBD-CTA-D, and
RGBD-CTA-F. Quantitative results are reported in Table 3. The FPS was
measured on Jetson AGX Xavier using native PyTorch FP32 inference
with a batch parameter of 1. The timing was averaged over 100
test images and included image preprocessing and inference threads
running in parallel with robotic arm, and gripper control programs.

To comprehensively evaluate the impact of multimodal fusion strate-
gies on seedling stress classification, we conducted comparative exper-
iments on three network configurations: RGB-CTA, RGBD-CTA-D, and
RGBD-CTA-F. Quantitative results are reported in Table 3. The FPS was
measured on Jetson AGX Xavier using native PyTorch FP32 inference
with a batch parameter of 1. The timing was averaged over 100
test images and included image preprocessing and inference threads
running in parallel with robotic arm, and gripper control programs.

content.html:
The performance metrics in Table 3 reveal the relative strengths of
the three fusion strategies in terms of both overall correctness and class-
level discriminability. RGB-CTA sets the baseline with a balanced yet
restricted performance across all four metrics. This outcome reflects the
information bottleneck that is intrinsically present in the single-modal
RGB representation when differentiating subtle stress variations. The
marginal improvements of RGBD-CTA-D over RGB-CTA indicate that
simply appending depth as an extra channel offers limited complemen-
tary signals. It gives some noise reduction or contextual help but lacks
an explicit way to integrate modality-specific semantics. In comparison
with the baseline model, RGBD-CTA-F achieves approximately 5 %
improvements in accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score. These en-
hancements serve to validate the effectiveness of cross-attention-based
feature-level fusion. By leveraging the complementary cues of RGB
appearance and depth geometry, the network can more dependably dis-
tinguish subtle seedling stress patterns (Sun et al., 2022). The consistent
precision and recall improvement indicates that RGBD-CTA-F enhances
positive identification accuracy. It also improves the comprehensive-
ness of detecting stressed classes, thereby increasing the F1-Score. It is
crucial for fine-grained multiclass stress classification where both false
positives and false negatives carry operational cost.

content.html:
Regarding computational efficiency and deployment feasibility, Ta-
ble 3 reveals critical trade-offs between model complexity and perfor-
mance. The RGB-CTA and RGBD-CTA-D models exhibit nearly identical
parameter sizes (18.09 M vs. 18.35 M) and inference speeds (7.6 FPS
vs. 7.4 FPS), reflecting their shared backbone architecture with only
minor modifications to accommodate the depth channel. This finding
indicates that merely adding depth as an additional input dimension
incurs only a negligible computational burden. However, it also results
in only minimal improvements in classification accuracy (from 90.9 %
to 91.2 %). This observation underscores the restricted effectiveness of
data-level fusion in harnessing multimodal synergy.

content.html:
From a computational perspective, giga floating-point operations
(GFLOPs) provide a more direct measure of workload than parameter
count alone. The GFLOPs increase from 8.2 (RGB-CTA) to 8.6 (RGBD-
CTA-D) and further to 10.3 (RGBD-CTA-F). This trend is consistent
with the architectural evolution from a single-stream backbone to a
dual-stream design with cross-attention-based feature fusion. While
RGBD-CTA-D introduces only a minor increase in computation by ex-
panding the input channel, RGBD-CTA-F incorporates parallel RGB and
depth encoders as well as cross-attention operations, which substan-
tially increase matrix multiplications and memory access operations.
The observed decrease in FPS is therefore primarily attributed to the
higher computational complexity and increased memory bandwidth
demand. In particular, cross-attention modules introduce additional
tensor reshaping and attention score computation.

Since Table 3 cannot fully represent the predictions for each class,
we further compared the performance of the three models using a con-
fusion matrix, as shown in Fig. 9. According to the rules for plotting the
confusion matrix, the numbers on the diagonal of each matrix (from the
top-left to the bottom-right) represent the correct predictions for each
class. The higher these numbers, the better the model’s performance
for the respective class. We analyze the confusion matrix generated
by the RGB-CTA model on the test dataset, as shown in Fig. 9a,
as the baseline. The RGB-CTA model displays significant off-diagonal
dispersion, particularly in intermediate stress categories (e.g., W4N0 vs.
W4N4 and W6N0), suggesting difficulty in distinguishing subtle visual
differences.

content.html:
The RGBD-CTA-D fusion approach treats depth and color equally,
without according precedence to modality-specific semantics or dy-
namic relevance. A more detailed analysis of the confusion matrix
reveals that, compared with the RGB-CTA baseline, the variety of
error types has increased, as shown in Fig. 9b. Consequently, this
approach results in information dilution rather than augmentation.
Specifically, several intermediate stress categories (such as W2N0-
W4N0) exhibit more frequent cross-class confusions. This implies that
the incorporated depth channel introduces ambiguities that cannot be
effectively resolved by simple concatenation. This discovery suggests
that naive data-level fusion may inadvertently intensify subtle inter-
class overlaps when the modalities are not adaptively coordinated.
Thus, it underscores the need for more structured fusion mechanisms
to clarify correlated yet distinct stress signatures.

A closer examination of the confusion matrices indicates that most
misclassified samples are concentrated in intermediate stress cate-
gories, such as W2N0, W4N4, and W4N0, where visual differences are
subtle and class boundaries are inherently ambiguous. These hard-to-
classify samples often share similar phenotypic characteristics, includ-
ing slight chlorosis, moderate leaf shrinkage, and comparable canopy
structure, making discrimination particularly challenging. In addition,
variations in observation angle may cause partial leaf self-occlusion
and canopy structure changes, occasionally masking discriminative
symptoms such as localized chlorosis or wilted leaves. Moreover,
forward–backward tilting of seedlings during robotic grasping can alter
the camera-to-seedling distance, introducing inconsistencies in appar-
ent scale that further increase classification ambiguity. RGBD-CTA-F
reduces these confusions more effectively under occlusion and scale
variation, indicating that cross-attention-based RGBD fusion improves
robustness by jointly leveraging appearance and geometric cues.

content.html:
In this section, we compare the proposed models with several open-
source lightweight classification networks in our dataset. The goal
of these experiments is to evaluate the deployment potential of our
method on resource-constrained embedded devices, emphasizing both
model size and classification accuracy. We chose models with parame-
ter counts not exceeding 50 M to reflect the practical need for a balance
between performance and compactness. The models were chosen to
reflect a spectrum of design philosophies (efficient CNNs, hybrid/resid-
ual architectures, and transformer-derived models). A suitable model
for real-world use must deliver high accuracy while remaining small
enough to run efficiently on diverse edge platforms.

content.html: 3.5. Ablation study: Effect of attention pooling module
content.markdown: # 3.5. Ablation study: Effect of attention pooling module
content.text: 3.5. Ablation study: Effect of attention pooling module

content.html:
The classifier part of the proposed method utilizes the attention
pooling module, which is an effective mechanism for enhancing the
model’s ability to process long sequential data. Attention pooling can
aggregate information from the input sequence, providing a com-
pressed information representation. It is particularly important for
dealing with limited attention spans. To validate the efficacy of this
design, in this section, ablation studies are carried out on the prediction
module. Specifically, the attention pooling module is removed from the
classifier section, and the variations in the model’s performance are
meticulously observed.

content.html: 3.6. Ablation study: Effectiveness of cross-attention fusion
content.markdown: # 3.6. Ablation study: Effectiveness of cross-attention fusion
content.text: 3.6. Ablation study: Effectiveness of cross-attention fusion

content.html:
To rigorously evaluate the impact of feature fusion hierarchy in
the tokenizer, we designed four ablation variants (tokenizer I–IV) with
progressively reduced fusion complexity, as illustrated in Fig. 12. Tok-
enizer I (Fig. 12a) integrates both shallow and deep-level RGBD features
via CA modules, enabling multi-scale fusion. Tokenizer II and III ablate
shallow and deep fusion paths respectively, while tokenizer IV serves as
a fusion-free baseline. All the ablation models are guaranteed to have
an output of 14 × 14 × 256 through a 1 × 1 linear projection, ensuring
consistency with the input interface of the complete model.

content.html:
As shown in Table 7, tokenizer I achieved the highest performance
(95.8 %), indicating that its strategy of fusing shallow and deep features
is effective. In deep learning, deep network features tend to be more
abstract and can capture high-level semantic information, and tokenizer
I can leverage these features to improve the overall performance of
the model. While tokenizer II’s performance (93.0 %) is slightly lower
than tokenizer I, it still outperforms tokenizer III (91.9 %), which only
utilize features from shallow fusion module. This further emphasizes
the importance of deep features in model performance. In contrast,
tokenizer IV lacks the CA mechanism and exhibits the weakest per-
formance (89.6 %). This indicates that the CA mechanism enhances
the model’s ability to capture key features by focusing on important
features and suppressing irrelevant information. The GFLOPs and FPS
values also reveal that the additional cross-attention fusion introduces
only moderate computational overhead while maintaining a practically
usable inference throughput.

shown in Fig. 12f–h. These observations provide intuitive evidence
that cross-attention fusion improves the network’s ability to capture
discriminative stress features from RGBD inputs.

content.html:
These results validate that hierarchical CA is essential for maximiz-
ing the complementary strengths of RGB and depth modalities. Shallow
fusion can capture coarse structural cues such as leaf edges and con-
tours, while deep fusion can focus on more detailed information. Their
combined effect fosters robust multimodal feature learning, enhancing
stress classification under real-world variability.

the query (primary feature) and depth features as the key and value

multimodal learning. This pattern allows the model to leverage depth
features to enhance and complement the information provided by RGB
features. In this design, depth features are not simply parallel to RGB
features; instead, they interact and fuse meaningfully with RGB features
through the attention mechanism. To validate the effectiveness of this
design, ablation studies were conducted, and the network structure is
as shown in Fig. 13.

attention guidance than the reversed configuration. RGB images in-
herently encapsulate rich semantic cues — such as color gradients,
stress-induced discoloration, and textural variations — that are highly
discriminative for fine-grained stress level classification. In contrast,
depth data, while useful for conveying structural geometry and spatial
morphology, lack the visual semantics necessary for precise query
formulation. When RGB features serve as queries and depth features act
as keys and values (RGBD configuration), the network learns to attend
selectively to spatial regions where depth cues reinforce or contextual-
ize color-based anomalies. Conversely, using depth as the query (DRGB
configuration) introduces semantic misalignment, as low-level geomet-
ric features struggle to effectively interrogate high-level appearance
features in the RGB modality. This misdirection compromises feature
integration and degrades classification accuracy, underscoring the im-
portance of modality-aware role assignment in cross-modal attention
mechanisms.

content.text: 4. Limitations and future work

content.html:
The CNN–Transformer-based algorithm was proposed in this study
for the classification of seedling stress levels, incorporating a lightweight
CA mechanism to enable efficient fusion of RGBD multimodal data.
Although the proposed method demonstrated competitive performance
in terms of classification accuracy, real-time processing, and embedded
deployment, several limitations remain that warrant further investiga-
tion for broader applicability and technical advancement.

content.html: 5. Conclusion
content.markdown: # 5. Conclusion
content.text: 5. Conclusion

content.html:
In this study, a lightweight CNN–Transformer framework was devel-
oped to assess seedling stress in real time during robotic transplanting
by integrating color texture and depth geometry through a dual-stream
CA strategy. The network employs a multi-scale tokenizer for rapid
feature extraction, transformer encoders for long-range context, and
attention pooling for compact classification. Model performance was
evaluated on a dedicated RGBD dataset comprising seedlings subjected
to graduated water-nutrient stress treatments and was benchmarked
against several compact vision networks as well as a channel-stacking
baseline. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed RGBD-
CTA-F model achieves an overall classification accuracy of 95.8 %
on a six-level stress dataset, while sustaining a real-time inference
speed of 5.2 FPS. Qualitative and statistical comparisons showed that
the proposed architecture delivered the most reliable stress-level pre-
dictions while keeping computational requirements within the lim-
its of an embedded Jetson platform. Future work will incorporate
model compression for ultra-low-power devices and cross-crop valida-
tion throughout the leafy growth period, thereby enabling continuous
vitality monitoring and more responsive nursery management.
